```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", message = FALSE,
                      fig.width = 6, fig.height = 4)
```

SIGNAL (**S**patial var**I**able **G**ene detectio**N** **A**nd c**L**assification)
detects spatially variable genes in single-cell resolution spatial
transcriptomics and classifies each one by the source of its variation:

| Effect     | Meaning |
|------------|---------|
| `CellType` | expression differs between cell types |
| `Spatial`  | expression varies over space in the same way for all cell types |
| `ctSVG`    | the spatial pattern is specific to some cell types |

This tutorial walks through a complete analysis of the example data shipped
with the package.

## Installation

```{r, eval = FALSE}
if (!require("devtools", quietly = TRUE)) {
  install.packages("devtools")
}
devtools::install_github("TingtHou/SIGNAL")
```

```{r}
library(SIGNAL)
```

## Example data

SIGNAL needs three inputs for the same set of cells:

* `counts`: a genes x cells matrix of raw counts (a base or sparse matrix);
* `location`: a cells x 2 matrix of spatial coordinates;
* `celltype`: a cell-type label for each cell.

`SIGNAL_example` is a simulated data set of 400 cells from four cell types and
70 genes. Genes 1-40 are null, genes 41-50 are higher in cell type CT1, genes
51-60 are higher in a central hotspot for every cell type, and genes 61-70 are
higher in the hotspot for CT1 only (ctSVGs).

```{r}
data(SIGNAL_example)
counts <- SIGNAL_example$counts
location <- SIGNAL_example$location
celltype <- SIGNAL_example$celltype

dim(counts)
head(location, 3)
table(celltype)
```

## Step 1: create a SIGNAL object

```{r}
obj <- createSIGNALobject(counts = counts, location = location,
                          celltype = celltype, project = "Example")
obj
```

## Step 2: filter and transform expression

Genes expressed in fewer than `min_cells` cells are removed. Each remaining
gene is converted to normal scores, `qnorm((rank(y) - 0.5) / n)`, with tied
zeros broken at random and the scores averaged over `n_imp` draws; `seed`
makes this reproducible. `transform = "rank"` gives tied counts their average
rank instead (deterministic, as in the original real-data analyses, but the
spatial test can be anti-conservative). `filter = "celina"` applies CELINA's
gene and cell filter instead of `min_cells`.

```{r}
obj <- SIGNAL_preprocess(obj, min_cells = 10, seed = 1)
```

## Step 3: build kernels

`SIGNAL_kernel()` builds the cell-type kernel and, from the coordinates, a
panel of 11 spatial kernels. These are 5 Gaussian and 5 Matérn kernels at
different scales, plus a thin-plate spline kernel. See
`?build_spatial_kernels` for the definitions.

```{r}
obj <- SIGNAL_kernel(obj)
names(obj@spatial_kernels)
```

To use other spatial kernels, pass a list of n x n matrices:
`SIGNAL_kernel(obj, kernels = my_kernels)`.

## Step 4: test genes

For each gene and each spatial kernel, SIGNAL fits

$$y \sim N\left(0,\ \tau_1 K_{celltype} + \tau_2 K_{spatial} + \tau_3 K_{interaction} + \sigma^2 I\right)$$

and computes four p-values:

* an **overall** test of $\tau_1 = \tau_2 = \tau_3 = 0$;
* a **cell-type** test ($\tau_1$), a **spatial** test ($\tau_2$) and a
  **ctSVG** test ($\tau_3$).

P-values are combined across the 11 kernels with the Cauchy combination test.
By default (`method = "davies"`), as in the code used for the simulation
studies, all four tail probabilities use Davies' method. `method = "liu"` uses
Liu's moment-matching approximation instead, and `method = "davies_liu"` (the
original real-data analysis code) uses Davies for the overall test and Liu for
the other three.

The result is a table with one row per gene and the four p-values, not
adjusted for multiple testing:

```{r}
obj <- SIGNAL_test(obj, ncores = 2)
obj
head(obj@result)
```

Compare with the true gene types: the share of genes of each type with
p < 0.05 in each test.

```{r}
type <- SIGNAL_example$gene_type[rownames(obj@result)]
round(apply(obj@result < 0.05, 2, function(x) tapply(x, type, mean)), 2)
```

Null genes are rarely detected. Cell-type genes are detected by the cell-type
test and spatial genes by the spatial test. The ctSVGs are detected by the
ctSVG test, and most also by the cell-type test. That is expected: expression
that is higher in the hotspot for CT1 only also makes CT1's average expression
higher than the other cell types'.

## Visualise genes

```{r, fig.height = 3}
SIGNAL_plotGene(obj, "gene51")
```

```{r, fig.width = 7, fig.height = 5}
SIGNAL_plotGene(obj, "gene61", by_celltype = TRUE)
```

`gene51` is high in the hotspot for every cell type. `gene61` is high in the
hotspot only for CT1.

## Step 5: find the cell types behind each ctSVG

`SIGNAL_celltype()` tests each ctSVG once per cell type, using an interaction
kernel built from that cell type alone. Here it tests the genes with a ctSVG
p-value below 0.05:

```{r}
ctsvg <- rownames(obj@result)[obj@result$p_ctSVG < 0.05]
obj <- SIGNAL_celltype(obj, genes = ctsvg, ncores = 2)
signif(obj@celltype_result, 2)
```

The small p-values are in the CT1 column, the cell type that carries the
simulated pattern.

## One-step analysis

`SIGNAL()` runs steps 1-4 in one call:

```{r, eval = FALSE}
obj <- SIGNAL(counts, location, celltype)
```

## Large data sets

* With more than 6,000 cells, `SIGNAL_kernel()` builds one Gaussian spatial
  kernel instead of 11, as in CELINA's approximation mode, which cuts run
  time and memory about 11-fold. Its bandwidth is CELINA's default
  (Silverman's rule on log-normalized expression); set it with `bandwidth`.
  Use `approximation = FALSE` to keep the 11 kernels, `approximation = TRUE`
  to use one kernel for any data size, or change the threshold with
  `max_cells`.
* With the default `method = "davies"`, every test needs an n x n
  eigendecomposition per gene and kernel, so run time grows with both the
  number of cells n and the number of genes. For large data, split the genes
  into batches (for example one HPC job per batch) and run each batch with
  `SIGNAL()` on that subset of rows of `counts`.
* `method = "liu"` uses Liu's approximation for all four tests, computed
  once per kernel. Its cost hardly depends on the number of genes, which makes
  it useful for a quick first pass. It can lose power for the ctSVG test when
  cell types and spatial domains overlap strongly.
* Memory holds the 11 spatial kernels plus working n x n matrices, a few GB at
  n = 5,000.
* `SIGNAL_test()` splits the genes over all available cores by default
  (`ncores`; on Slurm the cores of the allocation), with a progress bar for
  each spatial kernel. The workers are forked and share each kernel's set-up,
  so each adds only a few n x n matrices of memory. Windows cannot fork, so
  there the genes run on one core; use Linux (e.g. WSL or a cluster) for
  parallel runs. With a multithreaded BLAS such as OpenBLAS, set
  `OPENBLAS_NUM_THREADS=1` before starting R so that the workers do not
  compete for cores. `parallel = "kernels"` processes the spatial kernels in
  parallel instead (more memory per worker).
* R linked to an optimised BLAS (OpenBLAS, Intel MKL, Apple Accelerate) speeds
  up the matrix products considerably.

```{r}
sessionInfo()
```
